name: serialized-entity
intent: Store a whole entity as one serialized payload in a single column instead of mapping each field to its own column, so the object travels as one unit and its internal shape can change without per-field schema work.
problem: The persisted form of an entity is re-invented as columns for every attribute, so each field change means a migration and each read means joining or assembling the parts - while some entities (settings, imported payloads, plugin state, snapshots) have no stable field set at all and are never queried field by field. The catalog trigger: store the whole entity serialised rather than column-mapped.
context: Relational or document stores that offer a BLOB/BYTEA or JSON/JSONB column, an entity whose value is the whole object rather than its individual fields, and a persistence layer that can hook a codec into the mapping. Applies where the entity is read and written as a unit, where nothing inside it must be joined or constrained by the database, and where the team accepts payload-format versioning as an explicit obligation.
benefits: One row read or write moves the whole entity: no join assembly, no per-field mapper code and no partial state to reconcile.
The entity's shape can change without DDL on the inside: adding or removing a payload field needs no migration because the column type does not change (with a versioned reader).
Identity, optimistic-lock token and lifecycle columns stay explicit, so identity maps, version checks and foreign keys to the entity keep working.
Modern engines keep the payload partly queryable - jsonb containment, path filters and GIN indexes - so a serialized entity is not automatically a write-only blob.
Fits genuinely schemaless or externally owned structures: user settings, extension state, imported documents and snapshots, where a column per field would be speculative.
Compact for sparse or deeply nested data: one row instead of many nullable columns or child tables, and no ORM mapping for the internal graph.
tradeoffs: The payload is opaque to the database: no constraints, indexes, joins or referential integrity inside it, so field-level querying depends on the engine's JSON operators and cannot be assumed.
Every edit rewrites the whole row, so concurrent updates lose each other unless a separate version column drives optimistic locking; large documents also increase lock contention and I/O.
Payload evolution becomes the team's problem: renaming a field, moving a class or switching a codec makes old rows unreadable unless the payload carries a version and the reader still understands it.
Native object serialization binds rows to a language, runtime and often a library version, and deserializing stored bytes is an execution path for anyone who can write to the column.
Tooling stops seeing inside the entity: migrations, generated schemas, analytical SQL, masking rules and ORM dirty checking all treat the payload as one opaque value.
Loads are all-or-nothing: the full payload is fetched and parsed even when a single field is needed.

participants.responsibility: The domain object whose state is stored as one unit; it carries its fields but no persistence knowledge, and its identity and version remain outside the payload.
Converts entity state to the payload representation and back; the only component that knows the payload's field layout and the owner of its format version.

The persistence layer's extension point that binds the payload to the single BLOB/JSON column instead of generating per-field columns (AttributeConverter, JdbcTypeCode/UserType, TypeDecorator, Valuer/Scanner, serializer tag).
The real columns that keep the row addressable and conflict-safe: primary key, optimistic-lock version, owner/tenant and timestamps.
Issues the insert, update and select for the one row and passes raw bytes or text across the codec boundary; it never rebuilds SQL out of payload fields.

use_cases: User or tenant settings and preferences that grow field by field and are always read and written as a whole.
Plugin or extension state whose shape is defined by a third party rather than by the host schema.
Imported or externally produced documents (partner payloads, ERP exports) stored verbatim for later reprocessing.
Aggregate snapshots for audit, undo or workflow state, where the historical view is the whole object as it was.
Session or application state keyed by id, where no cross-row query of the fields is ever needed.
Caches and read models rebuildable from a source of truth, so a payload that fails to decode is recoverable rather than fatal.

Django's JSONField is this pattern as shipped framework code: it encodes arbitrarily nested Python data into one model field (jsonb on PostgreSQL), takes custom encoder/decoder callables as the codec hook, and keeps selected inner paths queryable via KeyTransform lookups and GinIndex instead of per-field columns.

Hibernate ORM binds an entity attribute holding a value graph to a single JSON column with @JdbcTypeCode(SqlTypes.JSON), and EclipseLink's SerializedObjectConverter serializes a Serializable attribute to bytes in one BLOB - both are the Column Type / Mapping Hook participant supplied by the persistence layer.

Entity Framework Core's ToJson() maps an owned navigation (or complex property) so the entity's whole owned graph is stored in one JSON column while the key, discriminator and concurrency-token columns stay relational.
avoid_when: The entity's fields are filtered, sorted or joined individually - map them with a Data Mapper or Metadata Mapping and keep the payload only for the schemaless remainder.
The database must enforce rules inside the entity (uniqueness, foreign keys, checks) - those become application invariants you have to re-implement.
The entity is large or grows without bound (event logs, line items) - split the collection into its own rows instead; whole-row rewrites and locks get expensive.
Other tools - reporting, migrations, ETL, masking - must see the fields; expose them as columns rather than hiding them in a payload.
The data is genuinely document-shaped and queried as documents: a document database solves it directly instead of hiding the document in one column.
anti_patterns: Serializing ORM-managed objects (lazy proxies, session-bound collections) instead of plain data: reload fails outside the original session and the payload couples to framework internals.
Using native object serialization for untrusted or multi-writer payloads - whoever can write the column chooses the classes that get instantiated on read.
A "BLOB as a private database": stuffing a whole model into one column and then re-implementing queries and constraints in application code.
Appending to arrays inside a JSON column forever, turning one row into megabytes and every update into a full rewrite.
Shipping payloads without a version tag, so the first field rename produces unreadable rows and an emergency backfill.
Smuggling credentials or personal data into an opaque payload to escape the masking, validation and audit rules that operate on columns.
design_principles: Separation of concerns: serialization (codec), mapping (column hook) and identity/versioning are distinct responsibilities.
Information hiding: the payload's internal layout is private to the codec; callers use the entity, not the bytes.
Explicit over implicit: publish a payload version and fail fast on unknown versions instead of guessing at old data.
Keep boundaries honest: anything that must be constrained or queried belongs to the schema, not to the payload.
Single responsibility per component: the entity stays persistence-ignorant while the mapper owns the bytes.
best_practices: Put a format version in the payload from the first release and keep the reader able to decode - or explicitly reject - every version still in the table.
Keep the primary key, optimistic-lock version, owner/tenant, timestamps and every filtered field in real columns beside the payload.
Prefer a text/JSON codec or a schema-driven binary codec over language-native object serialization unless the store is private and trusted.
Bound payload size: split unbounded collections into their own rows or columns and treat the payload as one atomic datum.
Test round-trips against stored golden payloads, including at least one document written by the previous format version.
Document the payload schema next to the entity - it is the de-facto DDL that migrations no longer express.
On engines that support it, keep the payload queryable (JSONB with GIN indexes) instead of treating it as write-only.
sources: Crawford & Kaplan, J2EE Design Patterns (O'Reilly, 2003) - "The Serialized Entity Pattern", ch. 8 (Database and Data Patterns), section 8.3: a serializable data object plus a DAO that stores the object as a BLOB.

https://java-design-patterns.com/patterns/serialized-entity/ - Serialized Entity (also known as Object Serialization): intent, Serializable + DAO/BLOB example, benefits and trade-offs (deserialization risk, format breakage).
https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/datatype-json.html - jsonb storage, containment and GIN indexing, and the guidance to keep JSON documents small because an update locks the whole row.

https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/6.1/ref/models/fields/ - JSONField: JSON-encoded data stored in a single model field, jsonb on PostgreSQL, custom encoder/decoder callables, KeyTransform querying and GinIndex support.

https://docs.hibernate.org/orm/current/javadocs/org/hibernate/annotations/JdbcTypeCode.html - @JdbcTypeCode(SqlTypes.JSON): bind an attribute to a single JSON column through Hibernate's type-code registry.

https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/microsoft.entityframeworkcore.relationalownednavigationbuilderextensions.tojson?view=efcore-10.0 - EF Core ToJson(): an owned entity and its nested owned entities mapped into one JSON column.

https://eclipse.dev/eclipselink/api/2.5/org/eclipse/persistence/mappings/converters/SerializedObjectConverter.html - EclipseLink SerializedObjectConverter: a shipped JPA mapping converter that stores a Serializable attribute as bytes in a BLOB.

https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Deserialization_Cheat_Sheet.html - OWASP Deserialization Cheat Sheet: why reading native-serialized payloads back is an execution path (CWE-502) and how to restrict deserializable classes.
